In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence does not support the use of HbA1c as a diagnostic tool in the absence of other clinical information, and that it is a poor diagnostic tool in isolation.
the evidence supports a causal role of LDL cholesterol in atherogenic events and the prevention of such events by LDL cholesterol lowering.
the evidence does not clearly support the use of statins in diabetic patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the results of the study suggest that the influence of LDL cholesterol, but not of triglycerides, on Lp(a) concentrations may vary between different populations.
the presence of the Lp(a) lipoprotein is an important risk factor for atherosclerosis and that the Lp(a)-related risk is increased in patients with diabetes mellitus.
the results of the current study support the hypothesis that elevated LDL-C levels and/or elevated triglyceride levels in diabetic patients may be associated with elevated lipoprotein(a).
The main takeaway from our work is that
LDL-C and TG levels have a differential influence on plasma Lp(a) concentrations.
